blocks.html:
The recommendation

Two changes. One grows what the list earns, the other stops the list shrinking. They are priced separately and either can go ahead on its own.

  • Double the campaigns, 4 a month to 8. Ongoing, $300 a campaign. Your own weeks say it's worth $97,679 to $195,358 a year.
  • Build the two flows you don't have. A one-off $2,400, then they run for free forever. Worth about $100,070 a year, and they pay for themselves in 9 days.

Why: your campaigns are under-sent

Over 52 weeks, May ’25 to Oct ’26, you sent one campaign in 40 ordinary weeks and two in 5. The one-send weeks earned $6,494. The two-send weeks earned $10,564. The second send earns a little less on its own ($5,282 against $6,494), so there is some overlap, but it adds 81% of a campaign rather than splitting one in half.

You will see more unsubscribes. That is the trade and it is worth naming, because the rate and the count move in opposite directions. The rate per send falls, 0.29% to 0.22%, but a two-send week loses about 66 people where a one-send week loses 38. Across 48 extra campaigns that is roughly 1,300 more unsubscribes a year.

The question is what each one is worth. The extra send brings $4,070 a week and costs 28 unsubscribes, so you are trading one unsubscribe for about $148 of revenue. Black Friday week Nov ’25 is the same story at full stretch: 5 campaigns, $35,727, 127 unsubscribes against a normal week’s 38, and still the lowest rate on the board at 0.19%. The people who left were not the people buying.

blocks.html:
Why: two flows are missing, and they're the two that compound

You run 4 flows: Welcome Flow, Browse Abandonment, Onboarding Flow, Abandoned Cart. Every one of them catches somebody on the way in. Nothing catches them after.

1. Nothing happens after a purchase. 6,856 people bought from you in the last 12 months and placed 7,408 orders, so only 552 were repeat buys. That's 8.1 repeat orders per hundred customers, on a $737 average order. A post-purchase series is the one email nobody ignores, because they just gave you money. Move the repeat rate a single point and that's $50,538 a year, from customers you've already paid to acquire.

2. Your best flow reaches almost nobody. The Welcome flow earns $32 for every email it sends, more than any other flow you run. It sent 857 emails all year, because 1,311 people joined the list and most of them never got a full welcome. Your sign-up form is part of it: 289,986 people saw it, 1,424 filled it in, which is 0.49%. Rebuilding the form and the series so everyone who joins gets welcomed is worth $49,532 a year at half the rate that flow already earns.

What it costs and what it returns

48 extra campaigns a year at $300$14,400 · $1,200/mo
8 flow emails at $300, built once$2,400 · one-off
Year one$16,800
Campaigns, at half your evidenced rate$97,679
Post-purchase flow, at a one-point repeat lift$50,538
Welcome rebuild, at half that flow's own rate$49,532
Year one$197,749
Return on the spend11.8× to 17.6×

Every figure above is half of what your own account already produces, except the campaign range, which shows both. For scale: the 46 campaigns you ran in the last 12 months cost $13,800 and are credited with $306,783, which is 22 times the fee. None of this needs a new result. It needs the ones you already get, more often and from more people.

What doing nothing costs, and what doing half of it costs

Your list is already shrinking. 1,311 people joined in the last 12 months and 1,770 left, a net loss of 459. Campaigns earn money from the list you have. They do not build it, and at 8 a month they spend it faster: add the 1,300 extra unsubscribes above and the net loss is nearer 1,759 a year.

That is the case for doing both halves rather than the easy one. The flows are what refills the list while the campaigns spend it: the welcome series is the only thing standing between a new subscriber and silence, and a post-purchase series turns a buyer into a customer. Your sign-up form at 0.49% is the other half of that and the rebuild includes it, though nothing above counts a single extra sign-up from fixing it.

Left alone the arithmetic only goes one way. Each year the list gets smaller, each campaign reaches fewer people, and the customers who spent $737 with you once this year quietly become somebody else's repeat customers. The flows are a one-off $2,400 to stop that.

What it asks of your team

  • Nothing for the flows. We build them, you approve them once, they run by themselves from then on.
  • No new approvals process for the campaigns. Same monthly batch, twice the emails in it.
  • No new platform cost. Your Klaviyo plan allows 280,000 emails a month. All of this uses about 127,000.
  • No commitment to fill the calendar. 8 is a ceiling we're allowed to use, not a quota. If revenue per campaign or unsubscribes move the wrong way, we drop back and you've learned where your ceiling is.

Campaigns. 52 weeks of your own sends, May ’25 to Oct ’26, grouped by how many went out that week. 7 offer weeks and 3 peak weeks are excluded, so it is ordinary week against ordinary week and a sale can't inflate the step. A cadence is only quoted where you ran it at least three times.

The unsubscribe count. Your two-send weeks also went to a slightly wider audience per send (15,573 against 13,884), so part of the extra 28 is reach rather than frequency. We have left it all in the frequency column, which makes the 1,300 a year the pessimistic reading rather than the flattering one.

Flows. Order, customer, subscriber and form counts are Klaviyo events for the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, read directly from your account. The post-purchase figure is one percentage point of your 6,856 customers at your own $737 average order. The welcome figure is the gap between the 857 emails that flow sent and the 3,933 it would send if the 1,311 people who joined got a 4-email series and 25% of them dropped out of it part way, at half the $32 per email it already earns.

Revenue is Klaviyo's attribution on last click, which is the generous reading rather than the strict one. That is why everything here is quoted at half, and the case still stands at half. A holdout test gives you the strict number and we will run one if you want it.
